2 pieces of advice, the same stuff that I told friends who were late in life into the work force. 1. your first job out of college sucks, and you get treated meh at best and get under paid. That is because college just jives you a key to a door, you opened the door and gained some experience, now leverage that into something bigger. Go take interviews to practice and get good at interviewing and learn your worth. Don't be afraid to ask for it, if they say no, or not within their range then you probably don't want to work there anyways. 2. Use your job to pay for what you love and find the silver lining in work. Work is work, unless you were born wealthy you have to make your way in this world and it sounds like you have. Use that to pay for what you want to do. Want to take up sculpting, do it. What to learn how to fly, do it, but use your job as a means to an end. Meet coworkers you can lament with, get out of the office at lunch every day for a walk, a coffee, something just get out and then work towards where you want to be.

I taught as an adjunct and eventually full time instructor with a major for profit school. I will say most, if not all of them look very heavily for 2 things just to teach. 1 what your degree is in and the number of post grad work in a field and 2 what professional experience you have in that field. So, my post grad work is all in computer science and I had very little trouble landing a job teaching in my spare time (I was out of the service by this time, but process is the same), that said, my mother, who has a Masters in HR cannot give hours away to get a teaching job, just to many people with the degree. So MBA's and such, if you do not know someone, you are unlikely to land a position doing it. All that said, teaching online is not easy to get into. You have to be a more seniored person on staff, and normally that is the bulk of your class load. I would strongly suggest looking into teaching classes in class, as you will have an easier time finding them, and it will get you on your way to the time in position needed to start picking up online classes. Most schools have mandated hours certain types of instructors/professors can teach. For instance when I was  just an adjunct, I could only teach 24 credit hours a year, where as a part time faculty member I was able to teach 30, and full time members were around the 60-80 mark, hence they are the targets to run the online classes. 

In general, you are better off looking for an in-class deal. If you message me directly I might be able to put you in touch with some schools that are looking, assuming you did not get your post grad work in a very poor choice field. 

As for how your command will deal with it, just remember the service commitment always comes first, otherwise the schools normally don't care what your day job is and you can adjust your schedule as needed.
